title: Defensive and error-resilient design
idea: Defensive programming makes a class reject bad input and protect its own state; resilient design decides how each failure is handled: retry, fall back or fail fast.
points: Validate at the boundary with guard clauses, so bad data never enters the object.
Copy mutable inputs in and hand out unmodifiable copies, so callers cannot reach inside.
Retry only transient failures, a bounded number of times, with growing waits between tries.
Fail fast on permanent errors; fall back only when a stale value is acceptable.

steps.caption: The request enters. Guard clauses check the arguments before any work starts.
Input is valid, so the remote source is called.
A timeout comes back. It is transient, so the retry policy takes over.
The policy waits longer each time and tries again, up to `maxAttempts`.
Every try timed out. The retry budget is spent, so no more calls are made.
A stale rate is acceptable here, so the fallback returns the last good value.
The caller gets 1.17, marked stale. An unknown currency would skip the retries and arrive here as an error instead.

code.title: Guard clauses and copies
code.caption: Both classes get the same list. The caller then clears it: one object is emptied, the other is untouched.

walk.text: The leaky class keeps the caller's list and accepts negative hours.
Clearing the caller's list empties the leaky shift too: aliasing.
Guard clauses fail fast with a message naming the bad value.
`List.copyOf` takes a private, immutable copy and rejects null elements.
The getter can return the field itself because the copy is unmodifiable.
Each misuse is rejected at the door with a specific exception.

code.title: Retry, fallback, fail fast
code.caption: A scripted source times out on cue. The service retries, then falls back, but never retries a bad currency.

walk.text: A distinct exception type marks failures worth retrying.
A scripted fake replays a fixed sequence, so the run is repeatable.
The constructor rejects a zero retry budget and a missing source.
Bounded loop: success stores the value as this currency's fallback.
Only transient errors are caught. Waits double each try; real code sleeps with jitter.
Out of tries: return this currency's last good rate, or fail loudly if none exists.

pitfalls: An empty `catch (Exception e) {}` turns a failure into wrong data that surfaces much later.
Retrying a non-idempotent call, like a charge, without an idempotency key can bill twice.
Storing a caller's mutable list lets them change your state after validation passed.

quiz.q: A payment call fails with 'card declined'. What should a resilient client do?
options: Retry three times with exponential backoff
Return the result of the last successful payment
Fail fast and report the decline to the caller
Log the error and return a success status
quiz.why: A decline is permanent: retrying cannot change it, and faking success is worse. Retries and fallbacks are for transient faults like timeouts.

takeaway: Reject bad input early; retry transient faults; fail fast on permanent ones.
